newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries down at midday after Phila Fed index.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries down at midday after Phila Fed index.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were weaker at midday on Thursday, under a little pressure from a rise in a regional Federal Reserve bank's index of business conditions in its area.
The Philadelphia Federal Reserve reported that its business activity index rose to 25.2 in June from 1.6 in May. Economists had anticipated an increase to 7.3.
Several factors mitigated the negative impact on the bond market of the Philadelphia Fed index's rise, analysts said.
First, the Philadelphia Fed index's price component edged lower in June. Second, the series is regarded as volatile.

In addition, price dips attracted buyers. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond, for instance, was briefly down as much as 9/32. By midday, the bond had recovered to 99-2/32, down 6/32, to yield 6.70 percent.
Analysts said demand just below current price levels would confine prices to a tight range. Traders said hedge funds had been unable to push the market below 112-00 on the September T-bond contract.
The market opened slightly lower but gained ground after the Labor Department reported an unexpected jump in new jobless claims during the week ended June 14.
Labor said the initial claims for unemployment jumped to 347,000 from 339,000 a week earlier, defying economists' expectations that jobless claims would fall.
Economists said the data hinted that the labor market might be cooling slightly and would make the Federal Reserve even more comfortable about keeping interest rates on hold.
The Commerce Department, meanwhile, reported that the U.S. trade deficit stood at $8.36 billion in April.

The $8.36 billion trade gap was wider than the revised March deficit of $7.76 billion but economists said that the months of March and April taken together showed that the U.S. remained very competitive in world markets.
The trade data strengthened the net export component of second-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP), economists said.

"Consumption is pushing GDP along at a 0.5 percent to one percent growth," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo Mitsubishi. "But these trade data are probably consistent with 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent GDP growth in the second quarter."

"The trade numbers were surprising," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. "People are bracing for a wider trade deficit this summer because the Japanese are reporting wider surpluses. But ironicially, a lot of those dollars that go to Asia are getting recycled into the U.S. Treasury market."
Traders said good demand was expected in the Treasury's auction of $13.0 billion in 52-week notes on Thursday.
At midday EDT/1600 GMT, the three-month Treasury bill rate was unchanged at 4.94 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were each up two basis points to 5.09 percent and 5.35 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-13/32, yielding 6.02 percent.
Five-year notes were down 2/32 to 100-27/32, yielding 6.30 percent.
Ten-year notes were down 3/32 to 101-18/32, yielding 6.41 percent.
(( -- Ellen Freilich, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
